entries.title: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
entries.summary: French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween, as some 320,000 people nationwide took to the streets.
entries.content:
France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe

PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.

Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.

The marchers' grievances are diverse.

Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."

The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.

Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.

Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.

Police impose curfew and other measures

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.

In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.

Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.

"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.

Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.

Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

entries.title: Key takeaways from this week's political meeting in Beijing
entries.summary: The Communist party central committee meeting was focused on discipline and fighting corruption. It comes ahead of next year when Xi is widely expected to try to secure a fourth term.
entries.content:
Key takeaways from this week's political meeting in Beijing

BEIJING— China's ruling Communist Party concluded its most important meeting of the year, confirming the expulsion of 33 senior party members, as leader Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign continues to widen.

The political meeting, known as the fifth plenum, began on Monday and wrapped up on Thursday.

Of the 376 full and alternate central committee members originally named in 2022, only 279 attended – more than a quarter absent. Many of them are believed to be under investigation.

The focus of the meeting was on anti-corruption and discipline, but Joseph Torigian, a professor of Chinese studies at American University in Washington D.C., says the meeting sends another signal amid wide speculation that he will seek a fourth term in office next year.

"This is Xi Jinping setting up for the next party congress next year by ensuring that everybody is on the same page as him," he says.

The meeting reveals how much work Xi thinks his party still has to do to become a more effective, loyal governing institution, according to Neil Thomas, senior fellow on Chinese politics at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

That is something he said Americans should also pay attention to, because it impacts the U.S. calculus on how willing China would be to use force over Taiwan, the South China Sea and disputes with the U.S.

"The focus of this fifth plenum suggests to me that Xi is unlikely to take that risk until he feels more comfortable with the party that he leads," Thomas says.

Here are other major takeaways from the meeting:

Who's in and who's out

Among the 33 expelled party members are Zhang Youxia, formerly China's most senior military general and Liu Jianchao, a senior Chinese diplomat previously tipped to be the next foreign minister.

China's military leadership ranks has "almost completely been purged in the last three or four years," according to Thomas.

However, one man not only survived the purges, but has been elevated – general Zhang Shengmin. He has been a key player in Xi's anti-corruption campaign. At the meeting he was promoted to the Politburo, which consists of more than 20 of the party's top officials. His promotion, according to Thomas, reinforces the importance of anti-corruption work in the military.

"There's a lot of churn going on," Torigian says. "That raises questions about just who [Xi's] going to look to to fill in the ranks when there's a big succession coming up at the next Party congress next year."

Instilling party discipline

One of the key themes out of the meeting was strengthening party governance.

Xi is looking to maintain the party's conviction from one generation to the next by convincing people to "put the Chinese Communist Party at the center of their lives and not their own selfish interests," according to Torigian.

He adds that this is a topic close to Xi's heart on how a communist regime can "maintain its purity and not degrade and collapse" like many other communist parties have in other countries.

Tackling corruption to "pointless formalities"

Xi's anti-corruption campaign started when he came into power in late 2012.

Since then, 7.9 million individuals have been punished, including over 960 senior officials, Zhang Fuhai, Deputy Secretary of the Communist party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, told reporters on Friday.

"The fight against corruption remains serious, complicated, and eradicating the breeding ground for corruption remains a formidable task," he said.

Xi has also complained about excessive formalities and bureaucracy, which according to Torigian is party language for going through the motions, having lots of meetings "but never actually achieving anything."

At the same time, there will be more regular reporting from discipline inspectors to central authorities to add scrutiny on local officials.

But to avoid attracting the attention of the discipline system, local officials may play things really safe, leading to more inertia, less experimentation, and "may end up having the opposite effect to what Xi intended," Thomas said.

No insight gleaned at the plenum on Xi's successor

Few political watchers believe Xi will pick a successor at the next party congress, and nobody knows exactly what he will do when he is ready to step down, according to Torigian.

Full decisions from the meeting, and perhaps deliverables, are expected to be published in the coming days.

Additional research by Jasmine Ling in Beijing.

entries.title: A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance
entries.summary: Here are five things to know about the massive hack of the crypto exchange Binance — from how it happened to what it means for the sector.
entries.content:
A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance

It was the biggest cyber heist in history.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges, was hacked this week, with cybercriminals plundering more than $6 billion. Experts widely believe the hackers were a sophisticated unit within the North Korean military that has a track record of committing cyber heists.

The theft stunned the crypto industry and set off new fears about a sector that many critics deride as the "Wild West" of finance.

Here are 5 things to know about the spectacular heist.

So first, what are crypto exchanges?

They are akin to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) or the Nasdaq, but instead of trading stocks, investors turn to Binance and other crypto exchanges to trade digital assets such as Bitcoin.

A wide range of investors trade cryptocurrencies at these exchanges, from financial institutions and sophisticated traders, all the way to regular investors looking to make some money.

OK, so what happened this week?

At 4:05 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, hackers were able to access the accounts of investors who trade cryptocurrencies at Binance. It took only about 20 minutes for these hackers to make off off with just over $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies.

Ari Redbord, the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a crypto research firm that has helped Binance trace and recover some of the stolen funds, calls it "the largest bank robbery in human history."

"Imagine a world where someone could walk into a bank and walk out with $6.36 billion in stolen funds and then move those funds at the speed of the internet," he says. "This is bank robbery in the age of technology."

But a lot of details about the heist are still unclear, including how exactly the hackers were able to hack their way into the trading accounts of investors at Binance.

Binance, working with other exchanges and partners, has been able to freeze about $3 billion in stolen cryptocurrencies, effectively preventing hackers from taking full possession of its digital assets.

The exchange has also said it will pay back any customers who were victims of the cyber heist — though it's not clear exactly how it will do that.

Why do experts believe it's North Korea?

The level of sophistication and speed of the hack all point to a North Korean military hacking unit widely known as TraderTraitor. The unit was also responsible for what was the previous biggest-ever cyber heist, the theft of $1.5 billion from crypto exchange Bybit last year.

"North Korea has built the most sophisticated cyber capabilities in the world. They have a cadre of teams of professional hackers who are part of their military," says TRM's Redbord.

"This isn't just a commercial hacker who's looking to make some money," he adds. "This is going to be used for weapons proliferation and other destabilizing activity."

What does this heist tell us about the safety of crypto exchanges?

Researchers say it's too early to determine whether there were any major flaws with Binance's security systems. But they say the heist is a clear sign of just how sophisticated North Korean hackers are.

Meanwhile, crypto critics say the way Binance and other crypto exchanges are set up deserve scrutiny.

A unique feature of crypto exchanges is that people can buy and sell digital currencies such as bitcoin — and leave them with the exchanges for safekeeping.

This dual trust in the exchange makes them mighty tempting targets for hackers. And what's more concerning for critics, crypto exchanges also don't have to follow the same strict regulations that govern established Wall Street firm.

"You may trade on the New York Stock Exchange, but you don't keep your funds with the New York Stock Exchange. You keep it with your broker — and your broker is audited and regulated by the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)," says Amanda Fischer, policy director and chief operating officer at financial consumer advocacy group Better Markets. "And your broker has to pay for insurance that will make customers whole in the event that there's a cyber attack."

"So the regulatory framework for crypto is much weaker than what investors in the US enjoy in other markets," says Fischer.

Though Binance has promised to pay back customers who lost funds, it is not necessarily bound to do so according to current regulations. And many critics worry that smaller exchanges could struggle to pay back their investors in case of a hack, leaving these traders to suffer the consequences.

Doesn't this reinforce the crypto sector's Wild West reputation?

For many crypto critics, it does. They warn the lack of clear regulations for crypto executives could lead to perverse incentives at these exchanges.

In 2022, FTX — then the biggest crypto exchange — got into financial trouble after a period of intense volatility in the crypto markets, and the exchange dipped into their own customers' funds as it desperately tried to rescue itself. The company collapsed, and its CEO and founder Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud among other charges.

"If a trade goes bad, it can become almost irresistible to dip into those client funds. Just this one time is what they say, to cover their losses," says Fischer at Better Markets. "But we know that that can cascade into catastrophe for investors."

It's another reason why the massive cyber heist of Binance is raising so many alarms.

entries.title: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe over Senate candidate
entries.summary: The latest developments come amid allegations, first reported by The New York Times, that Democrats recruited a spoiler candidate in the toss-up U.S. Senate race.
entries.content:
Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots amid criminal probe over Senate candidate

ANCHORAGE, Alaska — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.

The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.

Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."

Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator. The owner of a boat dealership in the candidate's hometown of Petersburg who had donated to his campaign told The Associated Press that an FBI agent visited the business and wanted to know whether he had been misled by Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy. He said he had not and that "Everybody knows who the incumbent is."

Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."

The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.

State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot

Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot: "I am not interested in tricking voters," she said.

Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest.

The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.

Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy "will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity."

"To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.

Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation would be possible, writing that voters' ballots are commingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.

They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.

Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska's ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.

Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual

Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.

It's highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.

Trump during a rally late Friday in Florida said Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan should be prosecuted. He noted U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche was in attendance and said, "He's going to make his own decision."

Trump, then addressing Blanche directly, said of decisions regarding the case, "Todd, please make your own," and watched Blanche's response.

Trump added: "OK, he said 'yes.'"

Peltola, at a campaign rally in Anchorage late Friday, said she is "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." She said she doesn't need any help in winning the race outside of the support of voters.

She was asked before the rally if it was possible that someone on her campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan: "I have no idea," she told KTUU. "I honestly have no idea."

The Times story revealing the potential recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan was based partly on interviews with a former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired before the August primary. Asked about Rios by the station, Peltola said certain people are "gone for a good reason. If I could fire them again, I'd be happy to fire them again."

Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.

Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.

Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.

entries.title: Perspective: Forget the ballroom, we're headed to Cheesecake Factory!
entries.summary: Former President Obama caused a kerfuffle with his comments about President Trump's interior decorating at the White House. But maybe state dinners should happen at The Cheesecake Factory.
entries.content:
Perspective: Forget the ballroom, we're headed to Cheesecake Factory!

Food fight!

This week, the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain unexpectedly found itself in the political discourse.

During a campaign event in Ohio, former President Obama criticized President Trump's affection for gold decor, saying, "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent retaliated by having a French Dip Cheeseburger for lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House, telling reporters, "I had a great meal, always have a great meal. I would tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try."

But this latest partisan debate made me wonder. Why spend $600 million or more to build a new White House ballroom to host state dinners? Why not just host those esteemed events instead at the Cheesecake Factory?

Come to a state dinner, I've been told, and you kind of have to gulp down whatever yellow squash velouté or fricassée of fava beans a server slides under your chin.

But isn't America all about freedom, choice and options galore?

Cheesecake Factory restaurants have more than 250 items on their menus. Now that's America! Chicken and Waffle Skewers! Tex-Mex Eggrolls! Pickle Fries!

What says America more? The Dover Sole Meunière, served with Potato Pavé, Spring Ramps, Snow Peas, and Parsley Oil served to King Charles III at a state dinner this spring? Or the Cheesecake Factory's Buffalo Blasts: chicken, cheese and hot sauce stuffed into a spicy wrapper, deep-fried, and served with celery sticks and blue cheese dressing?

"I'm absolutely stuffed," I imagine His Majesty saying. "British troops in 1814 would never have burned down a Cheesecake Factory!"

When French President Emmanuel Macron received a state dinner at the White House in 2018, it opened with a Goat Cheese Gateau. I'd bet that wherever French officials travel, hosts push a Goat Cheese Gateau in front of them, saying, "You'll love it! So French!"

So I can imagine a French president saying, "Forget the gateau! I want Asian Chicken Nachos! Wonton chips, peanut sauce and fromage fondu? Le yum!"

Move state dinners to a Cheesecake Factory, and foreign heads of state might even say, "Give me that plate of Fried Macaroni and Cheese balls, and I'll sign any tariff agreement you want!"

entries.title: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
entries.summary: The Siena Drone Photo Awards for 2026 offer breathtaking bird's-eye views of our planet, revealing landscapes, livelihoods and human stories often invisible from the ground.
entries.content:
It looks like a spacecraft that settled gently onto a golden beach.

Off the coast of Bangladesh, an enormous vessel lies stranded on the mudflats, its steel hull partially dismantled as workers mill around it. This unusual aerial view of a tanker, specially designed to transport liquified natural gas used for cooking, electricity and transport, won photographer George Steinmetz the top prize — overall winner of the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards.

Each year, the Siena Drone Photo Awards highlight bird's-eye views of our planet, revealing landscapes, livelihoods and human stories often invisible from the ground. Here, we've selected some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs, focusing on the countries of the Global South.

In an interview with NPR, Steinmetz says he's been long fascinated by Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe, nearing the end of their working lives, are dismantled and their materials recovered for reuse. The photograph is titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal." Steinmetz sent up his drone north of Chattogram (Chittagong), along this 13-mile coastal strip, offering a stark glimpse into what this industry is like.

He was exploring the relationship between human populations and the environment for a book project and saw the industry as an extraordinary example of recycling on a vast scale.

Photographing it proved surprisingly difficult. The ship breaking industry has faced criticism from environmental organizations, human rights groups, labor unions and non-governmental organizations for its unchecked pollution, the leeching of chemicals into the sea and dangerous working conditions. Shipyard owners are wary of journalists and photographers. Local photographers initially warned Steinmetz that securing access might be nearly impossible.

Undeterred, he surveyed and photographed the entire coastline north of Chattogram with his drone, searching for a vessel that would make an especially striking photograph. He eventually settled on the liquid natural gas tanker. "The trick for me was to find the right ship, that was in a really interesting state of disassembly. And these tankers are very unusual boats. It just looked weird, like some kind of a spaceship. It takes workers a long time to break it down. And then they have to wait for the tide to be right so they can pull the pieces ashore. They have big winches and boats that they use to get the stuff ashore."

He was able to convince the owner of the tanker to allow him to photograph it. The timing of the drone photo was crucial. Steinmetz wanted to capture the vessel at low tide, when the surrounding mudflats were exposed and workers could be seen moving around its enormous hull. Their tiny figures would look like ants, giving viewers a sense of the ship's mammoth scale. He spent several days photographing the vessel, returning as the tides shifted and the workers continued to take the ship apart for scrap metal.

After graduating from Stanford with a degree in geophysics in 1979, Steinmetz had first dreamed of photographing landscapes from above while hitchhiking across Africa, often traveling on the roofs of trucks.

In 1996, National Geographic agreed to finance an aerial photography project around the Sahara, for which Steinmetz learned to fly a motorized paraglider. "It was like being in a flying lawn chair or [sitting on] the front of a spoon," he says. Drones have now completely transformed aerial photography, allowing photographers to capture the world from perspectives that were once difficult, expensive or impossible to achieve, Steinmetz says.

Today, armed with a drone rather than a paraglider, he continues to explore how a view from the sky can reveal stories that remain invisible from the ground.

Southern Turkey: Carpet Fields

Why would anyone spread hundreds of beautiful carpets across open fields, leaving them exposed to a blazing Mediterranean sun for weeks or even months?

In southern Türkiye, this is part of a traditional process that gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. Under the intense sunlight, the vibrant reds, blues and other hues gradually mellow into glowing, muted tones.

For Ankara-based documentary photographer and lawyer Dilek Yurdakul, the drone was not simply a technical choice. It was an essential storytelling tool. "I wanted to create an image that first attracts the viewer through its beauty but then invites them to look deeper, to discover the people, traditions and cultural memory behind it," she says. The photograph won first place in the contest's People section.

Yurdakul traveled six hours in blistering heat from Ankara to the Döşemealtı district of Antalya to capture this spectacle. "The first sight was astonishing. The fields were far larger than I had imagined. Thousands of carpets and kilims in different colors, sizes and patterns stretched across an enormous landscape," she says. From above, the carpets resemble a giant patchwork quilt, almost as if melded together, but her photograph captures the shadows between these slices of color.

The aerial perspective allowed her to bring together several layers of the story in a single frame, she says: the artistic richness of Anatolian craftsmanship, the scale of the landscape and the human labor that connects them.

"For me, this was a visual metaphor for the invisibility of labor. In many societies, the people whose work sustains everyday life remain largely unseen and unrecognized."

East Java, Indonesia: Tumpak Sewu's Majestic Waterfall

In this photo, highly commended in the Nature category, an imposing horseshoe-shaped waterfall spills over the cliffs of East Java, Indonesia, at sunrise. Boston-based, French-British drone photographer Colas Decloitre had hoped to capture the interesting shape of the waterfall with Mount Semeru rising behind it. What he hadn't anticipated was catching the active volcano behind the waterfall, glowing red and writhed with ash, in the middle of an eruption.

"The only way to get the right alignment of the waterfall and the volcano is with a drone, as you can only be on the side of the waterfall yourself," he says. Using his drone, he could position the waterfall against the volcano, revealing an intriguing landscape that could only be viewed from the air.

Argentine Puna: The Last Ember

It looks like the glowing eye of a fiery monster.

It's actually a volcanic cone, the pile of rock, ash and hardened lava that builds up around the mouth of the volcano over time.

The Last Ember, by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi, is an example of how a drone photo has the power to transform landscapes into a dream-like quality. It was a commended entry in the Nature category.

The photo was taken in the Argentine Puna, a vast, remote, high-altitude plateau in the Andes of northwestern Argentina: a landscape of volcanoes, ancient lava fields, salt flats and desert mountains. The cone's reddish color comes from iron-bearing minerals in the volcanic rock, while the surrounding dark terrain consists of lava that cooled and hardened long ago.

Exploring these volcanic landscapes requires careful planning, long journeys across remote terrain and constant attention to the conditions. "At high elevations, the thin air and rapidly changing weather can also make drone operations more demanding," Tabacchi says.

Her winning photo was a case of serendipity.

"I captured it during an exploratory flight, while studying the volcanic landscape and experimenting with different compositions," she says. "It wasn't even photographed during the golden hour [shortly after sunrise or before sunset] which is usually the time I prefer for landscape photography."

"When I reviewed my photographs, I found myself much more attracted to this earlier composition. There was something about the geometry of the lava field, the small red cone and the immense volcanic wilderness surrounding it that felt far more powerful to me than the warmer, more traditionally dramatic light of the other photograph."

It reminded Tabacchi of an important lesson she learned throughout her photographic career: Extraordinary landscapes don't always need extraordinary light to create a compelling image.

"Sometimes the strength of a photograph comes from the subject itself, its shapes, its geological history and the unexpected perspective from which we discover it," she says.

Lake Natron: What Lies Beneath

Another commended entry in the Nature category is Holly Kirkland's "What Lies Beneath."' At first glance, it looks like someone splashed ink over a canvas. But what seem like tiny specks of ink are actually lesser flamingos flying over Lake Natron, near the Tanzania–Kenya border. A former kindergarten teacher from Delaware, Kirkland is a self-taught photographer and plans to relocate to Kenya in the year ahead to build a larger body of aerial work.

This photo wasn't taken with a drone. (Siena does accept other aerial photography entries in the drone category). Kirkland took the shot on a Sony A1 Mark II with a 70-200mm f/2.8 lens while hovering over the landscape in a helicopter, strapped into her seat with the door flung open.

The photograph reflects the ecosystem of the Rift Valley soda lakes — highly alkaline environments where these birds thrive as the dominant species. They are called soda lakes because they contain exceptionally high concentrations of dissolved sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, the same chemical compounds found in household baking soda and washing soda.

These caustic waters would burn the skin of most other animals, but flamingos have evolved specific adaptations to turn this harsh landscape into a sanctuary. For instance, they have extra leathery, scaly skin on their legs to withstand chemical burns and specialized salt glands in their nasal cavity to filter out the excessive salt. It's an important breeding ground for these birds, Kirkland says, with an unusual landscape, like an entirely different world, with "painterly looking plumes of sediment under the surface of the lake."

"I've never seen anything like it," she says.

"I think that when you're looking down, there's just so many different layers of beauty that you see from above that you could never see from the ground," she says.

Kazakhstan: Alien Land

Another highly commended photo in the Nature category by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi, the Alien Land depicts the layers and patterns of deposited sediments, tectonic movements and erosion over millions of years — natural geological formations in Mangystau, Kazakhstan.

"My fascination with Kazakhstan began in a rather unexpected way," says Tabacchi. "I was flying from Tokyo to Rome when our plane encountered considerable turbulence while crossing Kazakhstan. I remember becoming curious about the vast country beneath us. In my imagination, it seemed like a land of remote, mysterious places, still waiting to be explored."

In 2024, she traveled there for the first time. The formation featured in Alien Land, which she nicknamed Jellyfish (their branching patterns reminded her of a jellyfish swimming through water), was the result of extensive research rather than a chance encounter.

"I spent countless hours studying satellite imagery, searching for unusual geological shapes and patterns in the Mangystau desert," she says. "Together with my guide and best friend Sav, I then explored the region in a Toyota Land Cruiser 4x4, trying to locate these formations on the ground. It was an extraordinary experience, turning shapes I'd discovered on a screen into real landscapes that I could finally photograph."

Mangystau is one of the strangest, wildest, and most mysterious places Tabacchi has ever visited. "There's something about its immense, almost empty landscapes that makes me feel completely isolated from the rest of the world, as though I'm standing at the edge of infinity," she says. "It's a feeling I find difficult to experience anywhere else: a mixture of solitude, freedom and wonder."

Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh: Rohingya Life Between Aid and Uncertainty

More than 1 million Rohingya refugees currently live in Bangladesh, primarily concentrated in congested camps around Cox's Bazar. Shahedul Islam Sadik, a student at the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Rajshahi in Bangladesh, says he has always wanted to tell their stories.

His drone shot of the settlements was commended in the Urban category . "I wanted to document how a humanitarian crisis had reshaped not only the lives of displaced people, but also [show] the natural and geographical landscape of their place of refuge. The photograph is therefore about more than population density; it also captures the visible consequences of a prolonged crisis," he says.

Sadik was struck by how densely populated and congested the settlements are. "What stayed with me most, however, was the sense that receiving assistance does not necessarily mean having the life one wants," he says. "Life in the settlements can feel confined, without the freedom they once had in their homeland."

He wanted viewers to notice not only the lack of physical space but also what it represents in the refugees' lives. "For me, the drone photograph captures more than overcrowding; it reflects a lack of personal space, freedom and room to breathe, both literally and figuratively," he says.

Bangladesh: Ferry boats, Dhaka

A burst of color and celebration fills the waterways of Dhaka, Bangladesh, as thousands of people make their way home for Eid, one of the most important festivals in the Islamic calendar.

Every year, the holiday triggers a massive exodus from the capital, as migrant workers and other residents travel to their hometowns to reunite with family. Ferries, packed with passengers and their belongings, become a vital means of transport.

For photographer George Steinmetz, the scene offered a striking contrast to his photograph of Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry. This photo was commended in the Urban category. From above, the crowded boats, their brightly colored decks and passengers' festive clothing create a vibrant patchwork against the river.

"I've never seen a ferry terminal like that," he says. Dhaka's Sadarghat Launch Terminal is widely recognized as one of the largest and busiest river ports in the world, frequented by 50,000 people every day.

"It's such a joyous scene," he says. "They have shopping bags full of gifts of food to bring to their families. When it's packed with people, I knew would be really epic. And again, it's like they look like ants."

Steinmetz captured the scene using a drone launched from the rooftop of a building overlooking the waterfront. But he almost missed the opportunity. The skies were overcast, and rain began falling shortly after his drone made the photograph. Had the rain started any earlier, he might have been unable to fly his drone.

For Steinmetz, drones offer the freedom to explore a scene from different angles, searching for the perfect composition rather than settling for the first striking view.

"I don't just want to get a picture. I want to get the best possible picture," he says.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times , The British Medical Journal , the BBC, The Guardian  and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Do you have seasonal affective disorder? How to tell — and what to do about it
entries.summary: The syndrome can make people feel like a "hibernating bear," says Dr. Norman Rosenthal, who published the first research on SAD. He explains how to identify the symptoms and what to do to feel better.
entries.content:
This story was originally published on Oct. 23, 2020, and has been updated.

When psychiatrist Dr. Norman Rosenthal moved to the United States from South Africa in 1976, he felt less energetic during the harsh winters.

Life Kit

Seasonal Affective Disorder is real. Here's how to get through it

He noticed other people felt the same way. "Just like the autumn leaves, they became depressed on schedule," says Rosenthal. "In spring, the condition reverses itself." He studied the problem, and published the first research on the syndrome and coined the term seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, in 1984.

About 1 in 20 people in the U.S. have SAD, and it typically lasts about 40% of the year, according to the American Psychiatric Association. If you have it, you may feel sluggish or depressed, oversleep, overeat, gain weight and be uninterested in doing things you previously enjoyed. Many more people have the winter blues, a milder version of SAD, where you feel like a sadder, sleepier or slower version of yourself.

With winter just around the corner, here's why you may feel this way — what you can do to feel better.

1. Recognize the symptoms

For many people, SAD makes things feel difficult every fall when it gets darker earlier, but better in the bright days of spring and summer, Rosenthal says.

One of Rosenthal's patients described themselves as feeling like a bear in the winter and wanting to hibernate. "So if you feel any identification with a hibernating bear, you might well have SAD," he says.

Women are about four times more vulnerable than men, and the condition is more common in the Northern Hemisphere.

While some people don't feel different at all when the seasons change, Rosenthal says others are quite disabled by it. People diagnosed with SAD, he says, are "people who would go to a doctor because the problem was bad enough."

Rosenthal says it can be hard to recognize a pattern, because the symptoms creep up on you. "For example, it might be a little bit serious in September and a little worse in October and a little worse in November. It's a bit like the story of the frog in the bowl that keeps getting warmed up, and he doesn't realize he's going to die because it happens so incrementally."

But, he says, recognizing your symptoms and taking them seriously are critical, because SAD can be debilitating or worse.

2. Let there be light

A fundamental part of the physiology of this condition is that some people just need more light. One often recommended fix for this is a SAD lamp. Rosenthal says these lamps generate light that's far more intense than indoor lighting — about 10,000 lux, a measurement of light.

This light is absorbed through the eyes, not the skin — but, he says, don't stare at it. Rosenthal says he places it so that the light is shining down on him, just like it would if it were a sunny day. "That's how we evolved to see light — with the heavens above and the sun shining down, so that it comes and hits the bottom part of our retina." The morning is often the best time, and the earlier the better.

He says if you use the lamp for about 20 to 30 minutes a day, you should feel a difference within two weeks. If you don't, return it.

Studies suggest that the value of preventive light therapy is inconclusive and that it's really a patient's preference whether to use it or not. But as a treatment for those who have seasonal affective disorder, SAD lamps have made a big difference.

Remember, even if you use a SAD lamp, make sure you are still trying to get as much natural light as possible. Go outside, even if you don't feel like it, because even when it appears overcast, you are getting light from the sun. Remember that small things can make a difference, so trim any overgrowth around your windows and clean the panes.

3. Be thoughtful and consistent about what (and when) you eat

Rosenthal says people with SAD have a tremendous appetite for carbohydrates. "They crave sweets and starches. And needless to say, that puts on weight, and they can't always take it off in the summer, so every year they're ratcheting up a little more, a little more, and it's a real problem."

Emily Manoogian, a clinical researcher at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies, says people with SAD usually have a delay in their circadian rhythm, "these 24-hour rhythms we have within our body."Just like light, food is an important cue to your body. "If you are eating, your body thinks it should be awake."

Make sure to stop eating three hours before you go to sleep, so your body knows to rest. By just controlling the time you eat and keeping it within a consistent 10- to 12-hour window, you're giving your body a strong cue to tell it the time of day, regardless of anything else that's going on.

4. Make time for movement

Exercise is another environmental cue that helps signal to your internal clocks what time it is. It's a cue that says "wake up," Manoogian says.

"Exercising during the active time of your day can help your body know what time of day it is and stimulate the brain to be awake at the right time of day, then allow your body to rest in the evening," she says.

Rosenthal says when it's cold and dark and you don't feel energetic and aren't active, it can turn into a vicious cycle. "You don't feel like getting up in the morning, so you pull the covers over your head, so you get less light. So you feel more depressed, so you feel even less like getting up. Whereas if you force yourself to get up, then push yourself to do all these things, then you can feel much better," he says. So try to push through and get some physical activity.

5. Reduce stress

Rosenthal says seasonal affective disorder has three main causes: a genetic component, a lack-of-light component and stress.

Stress may come from a lack of motivation. "When you've got things to do and you're feeling down and not thinking straight and not feeling effective, that's when you can really feel most depressed," Rosenthal says.

So try to reduce stress as much as you can. You may want to decorate a room with bright colors and photographs that make you smile. You may want to see a therapist and talk through how you feel. You may want to try meditation. Rosenthal says the effects of practicing meditation and SAD haven't been fully studied yet, but he believes it can help. Be proactive about making pleasurable plans.

Rosenthal says a lot of people do really well following these simple tips. But if you don't find yourself feeling better or if SAD is interfering with your personal relationships or work, he says, medication can also be very effective.

And keep in mind that none of this will make the disorder go away, but as Rosenthal puts it: "It's not a cure, but ... sometimes the SAD dies of neglect."

This story was edited by Malaka Gharib and Sylvie Douglis. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.

Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter. Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit.

entries.title: After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces
entries.summary: In October, 2025, the remnants of a typhoon seriously damaged Alaska Native villages in the far western part of the state. A year later, one of the hardest hit communities is still recovering.
entries.content:
After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces

Last fall, the remnants of Typhoon Halong tore through numerous small Alaska Native villages off the road system in Western Alaska. The storm destroyed infrastructure, floated homes off their foundations, and displaced over a thousand people. A year later, hundreds remain displaced as the slow work of repair in a remote part of the state continues. And in one of the hardest hit communities – the small town of Kipnuk – people still aren't sure when they'll be moving back.

'Working as fast as we can'

The village of under 200 homes is situated on the wide open tundra and only consistently accessible by plane.

A year ago, 90% of the residences here were damaged by the remnants of Typhoon Halong, according to the State of Alaska's Emergency Operations Center. Dozens were swept off their foundations, some with families still inside. The community is now largely scattered across Alaska – some outside the region their ancestors have lived in for thousands of years.

Throughout the past year, crews have been working on repairs.

On a clear day in August, Eddie Chuckwuk's construction crew attempted what sounded like magic: raising a building back onto its foundations using air compressors.

Chuckwuk is one of several dozen people who have been working long days to rebuild the place where he grew up.

"We're working as fast as possible as we can to get the people back in town," Chuckwuk says. "That's what I just want to see – for everybody to come back and enjoy where they grew up instead of being placed in a different place … where they're not used to. It's pretty hard."

Challenges remain in moving back

This work is critical to getting Kipnuk's homes in shape to live in again, but the town is far from being fully restored.

According to the state, most people in Kipnuk didn't have home or flood insurance. They estimate that funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency will make most of the homes livable by Thanksgiving – meaning replacing wet insulation and repairing windows, doors and roofs. But the funds won't be enough to return some severely damaged homes to how they were before the storm. The state is currently appealing for additional funding to build replacement housing.

There's also no estimate on when the school will reopen.

Leona Paul, who has been working as a cook to feed the construction teams, says even if the houses are habitable, some people were too traumatized by the storm to return.

"I think it's too overwhelming for them," she says, "especially the older people."

And climate change is making towns like Kipnuk more vulnerable to future storms. Most people in town want to rebuild the village somewhere safer but the funding they have received so far from FEMA can only go towards restoring what was damaged. Kipnuk hasn't yet found the money to move.

Living away from home takes a toll

Right now residents may not have a better option other than moving back. Many say living in bigger towns, or cities like Anchorage, has been tough. People aren't speaking as much Yugtun – the native language. They're farther from loved ones. Their kids, who are used to playing all over town, have to watch out for cars.

Leona Paul, who spent part of the summer in Kipnuk, says she likes being there. "You're free to do anything you want," she says. "In a city you just can't do whatever you want."

Being displaced from the village has also meant separation from the Alaska Native cultural practices of hunting and gathering traditional food on the land.

Some residents, like Burt Paul's family, traveled home for the summer to practice subsistence and be together.

Upriver from Kipnuk on a lush tundra bluff, his family filled buckets with sweet, orange salmonberries, or naunraqs as they are called in coastal Yugtun. He says after last fall's destruction – he didn't know when he'd see these native plants growing again.

"It beats my mind that I see food growing, grass growing, fish coming in," he says.

Paul's family evacuated after the storm, but he stayed behind in Kipnuk, acting as a community leader through the aftermath. Usually, his family goes camping and berry picking for days. This summer, their trips were shorter – confined to when everyone was in town.

Short as those trips may have been, he says they were important: "We have to keep things going some way, somehow, no matter what situation we go through," he says.

He's not sure when his family – or his village – will all be back together again.

entries.title: Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms
entries.summary: Ahead of Election Day, listeners send in questions about whether debates are dead, if polls are reliable for election coverage and how Trump might work with Democrats if they win control of Congress.
entries.content:
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

Ahead of Election Day, there are a lot of questions about what might happen, what the implications of different outcomes might be and even what it's like to cover elections. In collaboration with the NPR Politics Podcast, listeners sent in their questions about the election and politics for our political correspondents to answer.

Many political polls have been wrong recently. How can you as a reporter provide an accurate news piece utilizing poll results?

This is a common question every election cycle, but it's a little like saying, "I don't like the media because the media is biased." There are good polls and bad polls just like there are good reporters and bad reporters.

There have no doubt been some high-profile misses, particularly at the state level. National polls have actually been pretty good when it comes to the horse race, with a slight underestimation of Republican turnout. But remember, these polls have margins of error. That means a poll with +/- 3 or 4 percentage points is actually a range of 6 to 8 points. That's important because in a country with very close elections, the kind of precision that Americans expect sets up the polls for failure because they're not intended to be that specific. They set more of a fuzzy range.

State surveys have seen a lot of junk polls, even a couple fake ones this time around. So it's really important to pay attention to the quality of the pollster. The reason for this is because of the decline of local journalism. Local newspapers and TV stations just don't have the kind of money that national outlets do to pay for good, rigorous and frequent polling.

Horse-race polling isn't even the best use of polling. I talk a lot about polls, but you rarely hear me talking about specific margins between candidates, unless there's been a trend moving the needle in a certain direction. The races are close, within margin of error in many places, and that's all that really needs to be conveyed. Unfortunately, some outlets emphasize the horse race, but the best stuff is underneath. Are there trends over time with statistically significant movement on important questions and issues? For example, we wouldn't know how quickly public opinion moved on important issues, approval ratings, attitudes and how strongly people feel about those things without this data.

Also, for those who don't think reporters should use polls at all, understand that campaigns and corporations spend millions of dollars on polling to inform where they spend money, where they travel and what messages to use. They use the same pollsters you hear about externally. All that said, polling is one tool. It's not everything, and it should be mixed with historical context, reporting with campaigns, and being on the ground, which are all priorities of NPR's as well. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Do you prefer reporting on midterms or presidential election years? Are there unique opportunities that midterms have?

Presidential elections are certainly easier to cover in the sense that there are two sides who are looking to be in one job. Plus, regular people are very interested in presidential elections, as is evident by the decline in turnout from presidentials to midterms. But midterm elections are also consequential — and can be a lot of fun.

You get a lot of quirky candidates in down-ballot races sometimes with interesting storylines that might not see a lot of daylight in a presidential election, which is like a solar eclipse. Plus, I got my start covering midterm elections, researching the 2006 elections and learning about every single congressional race, and it was fascinating — the characters, the different types of places and economies and people in this very large country. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Reporting during the midterms is so much more fun! Rallies for presidential candidates have tons of security and stadium-size venues. A lot of sitting and waiting, using your camera zoom and being stuck in a press pen.

Tagging along with a candidate for House or Senate, especially early in the cycle, can be so much more intimate. This year, I've covered candidates at an antique shop, a farmer's market, a UAW picnic, a family farm and a smokejumper-themed brewery. There is more opportunity to see candidates up close, watch them interact with voters and even ask them questions. - Sam Gringlas, NPR congressional reporter

I personally like all elections, which is what makes a presidential year so great, you get a whole smorgasbord of contests. The top of the ticket certainly consumes a lot of oxygen but I've found you can often learn more about how the election is going by spending time with congressional candidates or even candidates for the state legislature. And, unlike midterm years, more voters are engaged, which makes for better voter interviews. But, please check back in a week and a half to see how my sleep debt is doing and whether I still say I "like all elections," because this may just be the light at the end of the tunnel pre-election euphoria speaking. - Tamara Keith, NPR senior political correspondent

Is there a race you're watching out of your own curiosity that may not "matter" at the national level?

Every race counts when it comes to the balance of power in the House and the Senate. But I have been joking that following the twists and turns in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District is now my hobby. I did a story about this race about a month ago and it has only gotten more wild since. It is a district that President Trump won by 14 points that hasn't been represented by a Democrat in its more than 40 years in existence. But Republicans ended up nominating a Trump-backed candidate with a ton of baggage who only moved to the district to run for congress. In an interview with me, he blamed his grandkids for one of his missteps.

Democrats nominated a former Miss Nevada turned state legislator, who has been running a very solid campaign. The retiring Republican congressman is using colorful language to trash the GOP nominee every chance he gets and announced that he voted for a Libertarian instead. So, it's just totally messy. The Republican is still favored to win but I am watching closely because I just want to know how this drama ends. - Tamara Keith, NPR senior political correspondent

There are a lot of redistricting ballot measures before voters. In Maryland, voters are going to consider whether to [amend the state constitution which would ultimately] allow Democrats to add one more seat there. That one actually looks like it might not pass, which is surprising because this is a Democratic state. You'd think Democrats want to give their Democratic lawmakers an edge to create a new seat.

Coloradans are considering a ballot measure that would basically make it harder for their legislature to mid-decade redistrict, which a lot of other states did. And then in Missouri, they're going to be weighing another question about whether to allow congressional redistricting that would help Republicans flip a seat there.

Then there's Alaska. Every cycle they go back and forth about this primary system that they have and ranked choice voting. It is going before them again. It's always a squeaker. It's always really close. But voters have stood by their top four primary nonpartisan primary system and their ranked choice voting. - Ashley Lopez, NPR political correspondent

I'm paying very close attention to places like Michigan and Texas and what they tell us about the Senate. There's a couple of really interesting House races that I think are going to tell us something, especially in South Florida and South Texas with Latinos and how they move in this election, because they're quite the swing group at this point. There are a couple of governors' races and ballot initiatives across the country.

In California, I'm really interested to see how this wealth tax ballot initiative does. There's been a ton of money, tens of millions of dollars spent on that, and it's going to be interesting to see if in a place like California that do tend to be the ones out front on a lot of these kinds of experiments, if it winds up passing or not.

I'm also curious about something like the Nevada governor's race. And Nevada is always a really interesting place because people have a real independent streak. You've got two candidates here in Gov. Joe Lombardo, the Republican who was elected in 2022, and he's going against the state's attorney general, Aaron Ford. There's been all this talk about crime and about Trump and the high unemployment rate. But then you dig into some of their backgrounds. Ford has had to talk about how, as a college kid, he made some bad decisions, including running into trouble with the law. I think the outcome there is going to be really interesting to see, asking voters whether they're going to take the dirt of what happened with somebody a decade or so ago versus the national political climate. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

How is the executive branch going to be affected if Democrats take one or both houses of Congress in the midterms?

Midterms tend to be a check on the party that holds the White House. The way that happens, first and foremost, is when there's split power in Washington, legislation comes to a standstill unless there's compromise and with only about 10% of congressional districts being competitive, there isn't much incentive to meet in the middle.

Some issues that have bipartisan support, like guardrails for artificial intelligence, could see progress. But the president is not in favor of restrictions on AI. The biggest effect of a Democratic House or Senate will be investigations and oversight of the current administration. One thing that could be politically tricky for Democrats is how far they go with impeachments, if they go there. Republicans paid the political price for their impeachment investigations of former President Clinton in the late 90s.

Loading...

Only twice since World War II has the president's party picked up seats in a midterm — once in 2002 after 9/11 and the preceding midterm in 1998. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Are political debates dead? And if not, when they are held, are they doomed to be ever more divisive at the expense of platforming policies as they have been in recent years?

In midterms, you have incumbents who are reluctant to get on a debate stage because they don't want to give a challenger oxygen and raise their profiles. The thing about debates is that sometimes people don't feel like they get a lot out of them, because politicians are talking-point machines. The job of journalists and interviewers is to try and get them off of those and to press on vulnerabilities so voters get a clearer understanding of what those candidates want to do and why they want to do it.

That's a real service to voters when done well, considering the only things voters see or hear from politicians otherwise is pre-packaged campaign ads, speeches or curated social media clips. Pressing them on their policies in a debate is an important part of the Democratic process, and a big platform for people who need to increase their name identification, so, no, I don't think debates are dead. In fact, I think with what could be a record number of candidates in this upcoming presidential election, you're gonna see a lot of debates. Just wait. – Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent.

What from this year's midterms are you watching as potential indicators for the presidential election in 2028?

Jon Ossoff's margin in Georgia. LOL. Ossoff has emerged as a dark-horse potential presidential candidate, despite his denials. They always deny they're running until they do. There are a handful of potential 2028 Democratic candidates who are governors running states where they are heavily favored to win reelection, people like J.B. Pritzker in Illinois, Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, Wes Moore in Maryland. What do they say on Election Night to give any clues about what they do next. Or will they simply say how proud they are of their records running their states, which, by the way, can be hints of messages for… 2028.

There will be lots to learn from how Democrats affiliated with democratic socialism or the very progressive wing of the party perform on election night compared to moderates in various places. That could set the stage for the issue debates in the 2028 Democratic primary. Also, how do Republicans run post-Trump? Do any start to distance themselves in the days and weeks following the midterms, trying to lay out a different direction, while walking the line to keep MAGA on board?

You can't really read into how states go in midterms to say whether they're going to be competitive in 2028. These are just very different electorates than much-higher turnout presidential elections. The margin for the Senate will be interesting for 2028 and what it means for the potential of a governing majority for the next president. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Thank you to Courtney, Nathaneal, Chad, Erin, Renata and Tyson for the questions.

entries.title: Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
entries.summary: Residents are fighting back against plans for a project that would span thousands of acres near the Monongahela National Forest and popular outdoor recreation, ski areas and dark sky sites.
entries.content:
Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia

DAVIS, W.Va. — Stretching nearly a million acres through the rugged mountains of eastern West Virginia, the Monongahela National Forest links some of the state's best known natural attractions. The vast area ranges from the ski slopes of Canaan Valley to the dark skies of Blackwater Falls and Spruce Knob and includes the small towns of Davis and Thomas that serve as gateways for visitors to the region.

For the past seven months, Kaleb Skelton, his wife, Ella, their 2-year-old son, Ryder, and dog Mabel have lived in a camper in this corner of West Virginia's "almost heaven." Kaleb is finishing a seasonal stint as a campground manager on a lake near Spruce Knob, the state's highest point.

On clear nights atop the isolated peak, they get to experience a river of stars in one of the very few pockets of darkness remaining in the Eastern United States. The area has become a draw for amateur astronomers.

During summer's new moons, Kaleb says, one in four campsites he oversees is occupied by someone with a telescope. He thought his family's cabin in eastern Texas offered "the craziest" dark skies he'd ever seen, "but coming out here definitely rivals it."

A dark history for 'Stump Town'

Those inky-black nights — and the natural beauty they shelter — are now under threat from what many residents see as a modern-day version of extractive industries like logging and mining that once defined the region. In a place where tourism, outdoor recreation and community are deeply intertwined, a gigantic power plant and data center campus in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all.

A stark image of the town of Davis from 1885, during the heyday of logging, is a reminder of that transformation. The photo shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.

They used to call it "Stump Town," says Kim Williams, president of the Snow Sports Museum of West Virginia in Canaan Valley. At the turn of the century, massive first-growth trees dominated the landscape.

Then, logging companies "came in and clear-cut the whole valley and everything around it," he says.

By the early 20th century, entire mountainsides of red spruce and eastern hemlock had been stripped bare. Then came the coal companies, which left the nearby Blackwater River acidic and dangerous to drink.

Today, the scars still show. The big trees won't return for generations, but a century of natural regrowth, conservation and deliberate restoration means the land is on its way to healing.

While few expect that the latest tech boom presages anything like the environmental destruction of the past, many see the proposed new Ridgeline data center as a big step backward, undoing the progress the local community has made to recover.

A roughly 785-megawatt generating plant is slated to be the first part of "a large-scale data and energy infrastructure project designed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and enterprise systems," according to Purcellville, Va.-based Fundamental Data LLC, the company behind Ridgeline.

The complex would rely primarily on natural gas, with diesel as a backup fuel source. Power generated on-site, rather than purchased from the regional grid, could ease some concerns about the project's effects on electricity rates. It does not, however, resolve concerns over air and water pollution.

Located on a reclaimed coal-mining site, plans are for an initial 291 acres that could eventually expand to 10,000 acres — 15 square miles — and include parts of neighboring Grant County, according to local news reports.

Speaking to NPR, Casey Chapman, listed in court documents as Fundamental Data's "responsible individual," declined to speculate on the facility's ultimate size, saying only that "if fully developed … it would be thousands of acres."

Light pollution is a common complaint from residents living near data centers. Chapman says the company will use "well-designed" lighting to help minimize the effects of sky glow, in an effort not to jeopardize nearby Blackwater Falls State Park's pursuit of an official dark-sky certification.

An analysis by the Northern Virginia Astronomy Club, which hosts an annual star party in the region, found that Ridgeline's initial footprint could increase sky glow near Blackwater by 528%, transforming its nighttime rural sky to one comparable to a suburban area. (The same analysis found only a minimal impact on Spruce Knob.)

But safety and security — not light pollution — take precedence, Chapman says. The facility will be "an industrial plant that runs around the clock," he notes. "Crews need proper lighting to operate and maintain equipment safely."

Opponents face an uphill battle

Chip Chase is among the skeptics. He runs White Grass Ski Touring Center, a popular cross-country ski area that he helped found 45 years ago. He is a fixture in the local community that he describes as "Vermont, with Southern hospitality."

"If you're an outdoor person, this place is paradise," he says. "People come here to get away from data centers. People want dark skies here. People want to have a peaceful, quiet recreational area."

Economic development, however, is a top priority for the state of West Virginia. It ranks among the poorest in the country and has the unique distinction of having lost population since 1950.

John Deskins, director of the West Virginia University Bureau of Business and Economic Research, says data centers could be a boon. "As long as we're making sure that we follow all the proper procedures around noise pollution, water pollution, [and] other elements of environmental pollution ... I think they're a good opportunity," he says.

It is those proper procedures that worry people in Tucker United, a grassroots group opposing the data center plans. As in so many other places across the country, they are battling what they see as a lack of transparency.

The first anyone in the community heard about the Ridgeline project was March 2025, when an obscure notice appeared in a local newspaper announcing the request for an air-quality permit for a proposed power plant, says Davis Mayor Alan Tomson. A resident called him to ask if he knew anything about it. "I told her that I did not," Tomson says. He then called the mayor of neighboring Thomas. "He also had not heard anything about it."

From there, Tomson says, things moved quickly. A month later, the Republican super-majority in both houses of the state legislature passed a highly unusual bill exempting certified microgrid districts and high-impact data centers from county or municipal zoning or any local restrictions related to horticultural, noise, viewshed, lighting, development or land use.

A lack of guardrails

Opponents quickly gathered 1,000 signatures on a petition urging Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey to veto the bill. They were unsuccessful. Signing the legislation, the governor noted the state's need to "continue to focus on economic development and utilizing our many natural resources," adding that "companies will now be able to quickly build, expand, and increase job creation right here in West Virginia."  

"They completely got rid of any … sort of regulation or guardrails for these data center developments," says Tucker United spokesperson Nikki Forrester. "They want to sell us out, … extract our resources and leave us with the mess."

The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection approved Fundamental Data's air-quality permit without, according to Tucker United and other activist groups, conducting a comprehensive assessment of the facility's potential public-health impacts on the surrounding valley. When asked by NPR about Tucker United's concerns, the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection responded that it "does not comment on active litigation" and declined an interview request.

Opponents of the project subsequently commissioned their own analysis finding that the Ridgeline plant could cause between $19 million and $35 million a year in health-related damages and premature deaths.

Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club challenged the air-permit decision in court. Their appeal was dismissed in August on jurisdictional grounds. The groups say they will go to the state's Supreme Court.

Chapman says Tucker United's air-quality study assumes Ridgeline will emit the maximum amount of pollution allowed by its air permit for an entire year, when in fact the permit sets an upper limit and "we're going to operate within those limits," he says.

There are other environmental concerns. Forrester notes that Canaan Valley's bowl shape and temperature inversions can trap air pollutants near the ground. As for water, she says, "storing 30 million gallons of diesel right on a creek that feeds into our water supplies is really dangerous and puts not just our community, but every community downstream at risk."

Fundamental Data's Chapman says the storage would be safe and that all of the tanks would not need to be filled at any given time.

In addition to the potential environmental and health hazards, many residents find it particularly galling that West Virginia House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, a Charleston-based attorney with the law firm Bowles Rice, is listed as lead attorney for Fundamental Data in the permit dispute.

"Here's a guy who's writing laws [and] sponsoring legislation while under contract for one of the people that he's working for," complains Gary Berti, a retired homeowner in Davis. "To me, that's a conflict of interest."

In an email to NPR, Hanshaw stated: "I am not now, nor have I ever been, employed by Fundamental Data. I am a partner in a law firm. It is public record that the law firm of Bowles Rice is currently counsel for Fundamental Data in a litigation matter pending in West Virginia."

Jobs are needed, but at what cost?
